lead: An oscillator makes a steady RF sine wave with no input; a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) lets a DC voltage set its frequency. No oscillator is perfect: its phase wanders, which spreads some of its power into nearby frequencies, measured as phase noise in dBc/Hz. A frequency synthesizer locks a VCO to a clean crystal reference with a phase-locked loop (PLL), so the output has the crystal's accuracy and stability at any channel the divider asks for. These blocks supply the LO behind every mixer in a radio.
prereq: You need: LC resonance and varactors from RF passive components, and the mixer of mixers.

blocks.text: An oscillator is an amplifier of gain A with a frequency-selective feedback network β. At power-up, noise at the frequency where the loop phase is 0° (or n × 360°) and the loop gain exceeds one grows. As the amplitude rises the amplifier saturates, its gain falls, and the amplitude settles where the loop gain is exactly one. That steady state is the Barkhausen condition:

blocks.where: A is the amplifier gain and β the feedback fraction, both complex; to start reliably, |Aβ| is designed at 2 to 3 at power-up.

blocks.text: At RF the same idea is written as a negative resistance. An LC tank with loss resistance R<sub>p</sub> rings down; an active circuit (a cross-coupled transistor pair, or a Colpitts transistor) presents −R, and when |−R| ≤ R<sub>p</sub> the losses are cancelled and the tank oscillates at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). The tank's Q sets how pure the tone is. A ring oscillator instead chains an odd number N of inverting stages: the inversions give 180°, and the stage delays supply the other 180°, so the loop's total is 360° at f = 1/(2Nt<sub>d</sub>), where t<sub>d</sub> is one stage's delay. Rings are small and tune widely, but with no resonator their phase noise is far worse.

A VCO's output frequency is f<sub>out</sub> = f₀ + K<sub>VCO</sub>V<sub>tune</sub>, where K<sub>VCO</sub> is the tuning gain in Hz/V. In an LC VCO the tuning element is a varactor or a switched-capacitor bank. Because C(V) is not linear, K<sub>VCO</sub> changes across the band. A large K<sub>VCO</sub> tunes widely but turns control-line noise into frequency noise.
Phase noise L(Δf) is the noise power in a 1 Hz bandwidth at an offset Δf from the carrier, divided by the carrier power, in dBc/Hz. Leeson's model gives its shape for an LC oscillator:

blocks.where: F is the active device's noise factor; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K; T in K; P<sub>s</sub> is the signal power in the tank in W; f₀ the carrier frequency; Q the loaded tank Q; f<sub>c</sub> the flicker corner; Δf the offset, all in Hz. Some textbooks write FkT/(2P<sub>s</sub>) as the first factor, which is 6 dB lower; use your prescribed book's form.

blocks.text: Far from the carrier (Δf above f₀/2Q) the noise is flat at 2FkT/P<sub>s</sub>; below f₀/2Q it rises 20 dB per decade towards the carrier (1/f²), and below the flicker corner f<sub>c</sub> 30 dB per decade (1/f³). Doubling Q lowers the 1/f² region by 6 dB; doubling the signal power lowers everything by 3 dB.

A phase-frequency detector (PFD) compares the reference f<sub>ref</sub> with the VCO frequency divided by N. A charge pump turns the phase error into current pulses, a loop filter turns those into the VCO control voltage, and the loop settles when f<sub>VCO</sub>/N = f<sub>ref</sub>, so f<sub>out</sub> = N·f<sub>ref</sub>. In an integer-N synthesizer N is a whole number and the channel spacing equals f<sub>ref</sub>: channels at 2402 to 2480 MHz in 1 MHz steps need f<sub>ref</sub> = 1 MHz and N = 2402 to 2480. A fractional-N synthesizer makes the average N = N<sub>int</sub> + K/M by switching the divider between N<sub>int</sub> and N<sub>int</sub> + 1, so a high reference can still give fine steps; its price is fractional spurs, reduced by a sigma-delta modulator that randomises the switching.

Inside the loop bandwidth f<sub>L</sub> the output follows the reference, raised by 20 log₁₀N (phase is multiplied by N with frequency, and noise power goes as phase squared). Outside f<sub>L</sub> the output follows the free VCO. The lowest total comes from setting f<sub>L</sub> where the two curves cross. A wider loop settles faster (in a few times 1/f<sub>L</sub>) but passes more reference noise and spurs.

examples.question: A 2 GHz LC VCO has F = 2 (3 dB), a tank signal power of 1 mW, loaded Q = 8 and a flicker corner of 100 kHz, at T = 290 K. Use the Leeson model to find its phase noise at 1 MHz and at 10 kHz offset, and the offset where the 1/f² region begins.
steps: f₀/2Q = 2 × 10⁹/16 = 125 MHz: the 1/f² region begins below 125 MHz offset.
At 1 MHz: (f₀/(2QΔf))² = 125² = 15 625, so the second factor is 15 626 = +41.9 dB; flicker factor 1 + 0.1 = 1.1 = +0.4 dB.
L(10 kHz) = −168.0 + 81.9 + 10.4 = −75.6 dBc/Hz. Between 100 kHz (−103.0) and 1 MHz (−125.6) the slope is about 23 dB per decade, close to the 1/f² value of 20 (the flicker term still adds a little).
examples.answer: L = −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz and −75.6 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz; the 1/f² region starts below 125 MHz and the 1/f³ region below the 100 kHz corner.

examples.question: The same VCO is locked in a PLL with a 10 MHz crystal reference whose phase noise is −140 dBc/Hz at 1 kHz and −155 dBc/Hz from 10 kHz outwards. (a) Find N and the reference noise at the output. (b) Choose the loop bandwidth. (c) Give the output phase noise at 10 kHz and 1 MHz. (d) A fractional-N version uses a 26 MHz reference for a 2437 MHz channel: find N.
steps: Reference at the output: −140 + 46.0 = −94.0 dBc/Hz at 1 kHz and −155 + 46.0 = −109.0 dBc/Hz beyond 10 kHz.
The free VCO (−103.0 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz, −110.3 at 200 kHz) crosses −109.0 at about 176 kHz, so set f<sub>L</sub> ≈ 180 kHz.
At 10 kHz (inside the loop) the output follows the multiplied reference, −109.0 dBc/Hz, 33 dB better than the free VCO's −75.6.
At 1 MHz (outside the loop) the output follows the VCO, −125.6 dBc/Hz, 16.6 dB better than the multiplied reference.
examples.answer: N = 200 adds 46.0 dB; a loop bandwidth near 180 kHz gives −109.0 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz and −125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz; the fractional-N divider is 93 + 19/26.

traps: Treating dBc/Hz as total noise. It is a density at one offset; total phase noise (or jitter) needs an integral over the offsets.
Adding 10 log₁₀N for frequency multiplication. Phase deviation is multiplied by N and noise power goes as its square, so the rise is 20 log₁₀N: 46 dB for N = 200.
Saying a PLL removes the VCO's noise at every offset. It suppresses VCO noise only inside the loop bandwidth; far out, the output is the free VCO.
Stating the Barkhausen condition as gain = 1 only. The loop phase must also be 0° (or n × 360°).
Using f<sub>ref</sub> as the channel spacing of a fractional-N synthesizer. Its spacing is f<sub>ref</sub>/M, much finer than f<sub>ref</sub>.

quiz.a: In steady state |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0° or a whole number of 360°; at start-up |Aβ| must exceed 1.

quiz.q: Why does a higher tank Q lower phase noise?
quiz.a: In Leeson's model the term (f₀/(2QΔf))² falls as Q², so the 1/f² region drops 6 dB for each doubling of Q; physically a sharper resonance rejects noise at offsets from the carrier.

quiz.q: A 100 MHz reference has −140 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz offset and is multiplied to 2 GHz. Find N and the multiplied phase noise.
A VCO has K<sub>VCO</sub> = 50 MHz/V. How far does the frequency move for a 0.4 V change in V<sub>tune</sub>?
An integer-N synthesizer covers 2402 to 2480 MHz in 2 MHz steps. Give f<sub>ref</sub> and the range of N.
A strong blocker sits 1 MHz from a weak wanted signal. Explain reciprocal mixing and how LO phase noise sets the damage.
quiz.a: The LO's phase-noise skirt 1 MHz from its carrier mixes with the blocker onto the wanted signal's IF, adding noise P<sub>blocker</sub> + L(1 MHz) + 10 log₁₀B; a lower L at that offset, or filtering the blocker before the mixer, reduces it.

quiz.q: Why does a wider loop bandwidth lock faster but can raise the noise?
quiz.a: A wider loop corrects errors faster, settling in a few 1/f<sub>L</sub>. But inside f<sub>L</sub> the output copies the reference noise times N (plus charge-pump noise), so widening past the crossover with the VCO curve raises the total.

beyond: Not for the exam. All-digital PLLs replace the charge pump with a time-to-digital converter and a digital loop filter. Millimetre-wave radios multiply a lower-frequency synthesizer, so each doubling costs 6 dB of phase noise. Data links quote phase noise as RMS jitter. Search for 'all-digital PLL' and 'phase noise to jitter'.

figure.caption: The worked examples' synthesizer: inside the 180 kHz loop the output follows the reference raised by 20 log₁₀200 = 46 dB (−109.0 dBc/Hz at 10 kHz); outside it follows the free VCO (−125.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz). The loop bandwidth sits where the two dashed curves cross.

spec.aria: Phase noise in dBc per hertz against offset from 1 kilohertz to 10 megahertz on a log scale. The free VCO curve falls steeply, reaching minus 75.6 at 10 kilohertz and minus 125.6 at 1 megahertz. The multiplied reference is flat at minus 109 beyond 10 kilohertz. They cross near 180 kilohertz, marked as the loop bandwidth. The PLL output, drawn solid, follows the reference below 180 kilohertz and the VCO above.
